comp-fundamentals.topicName: Computer Fundamentals — Hardware, Memory Hierarchy, Generations, Number Systems
comp-fundamentals.whatItIs: The factual base layer of Computer Aptitude: what a computer is made of and what each part does. Hardware vs software, input vs output devices, the CPU and its units, the memory hierarchy from registers down to tape, the RAM/ROM families, the five generations and their defining technology, storage units from bit to yottabyte, and binary/octal/hex conversion. Roughly 40-50% of the Computer questions that appear in Clerk Mains come from this block, because it is the part that can be asked in one line with no context. There is nothing here to 'solve' except the number-system conversions — everything else is recall, and the only skill being tested is whether the fact is in your head instantly or not.
comp-fundamentals.coreMethod:
1. Build ONE double-sided A4 revision sheet for this whole module. Nothing else. If a fact will not fit on that sheet it is too rare to be worth Clerk-level marks.
2. Side 1, six boxes, drawn in this fixed spatial order so your memory has a map: (i) Hardware vs Software vs Firmware; (ii) Input devices | Output devices | Both (touchscreen, modem, NIC, headset, hard disk as I/O storage); (iii) CPU = ALU + Control Unit + Registers, plus what each does in four words; (iv) Memory hierarchy drawn as a triangle — Registers, Cache L1/L2/L3, RAM, Secondary (SSD/HDD/optical), Tertiary (magnetic tape) — with two arrows down the side: 'speed & cost-per-bit decrease' and 'capacity increases'; (v) RAM/ROM family tree; (vi) Generations table.
3. Side 2, four boxes: (i) storage-unit ladder bit → nibble(4 bits) → byte(8) → KB → MB → GB → TB → PB → EB → ZB → YB, ×1024 from byte upward (1 nibble = 4 bits, 1 byte = 8 bits); (ii) number-system conversion rules; (iii) types of computers (analog/digital/hybrid, and micro/mini/mainframe/super); (iv) a 'confusion pairs' strip — the traps list below, written as pairs, not as paragraphs.
4. Write the sheet by hand ONCE from a source book, then never rewrite it. Rewriting feels productive and is not. From then on you only test against it.
5. Self-test protocol — active recall, never re-reading. Fold the sheet so only the box headings show. Speak the contents of each box aloud from memory in under 60 seconds. Anything you stumble on gets a red dot in the margin. Three red dots on the same fact means it moves to a separate 'leech list' of 10-15 items which you read at the start of every single study day until it stops being a leech.
6. Spaced revision schedule: Day 0 build, Day 1, Day 3, Day 7, Day 14, Day 30, then once a fortnight until exam. Each revision after Day 7 is a 6-minute recitation, not a study session.
7. Question-bank loop, twice a week: 25 mixed MCQs from previous-year Clerk/PO Mains papers, all five options, timed at 15 seconds each. Every question you get wrong is not 'revised' — you find which box on the sheet it came from and re-recite that whole box.
8. Maintain an error log with exactly three columns: question, my answer, the pair I confused. After four weeks the log will show you have 6-8 recurring confusions and nothing else. Those become your last-week revision, not the whole sheet.
9. Number-system conversions are the one part with a procedure. Drill them separately, 10 conversions a week, until binary↔hex is grouping-by-4 on sight. Memorise 0000-1111 as 0-F cold; that single table kills every hex question.
10. Final week: recite the sheet daily. Do not add any new material to this module after the last week begins — new facts displace old ones under exam stress.
tricks: Memory hierarchy in one sentence: 'Registers are inside the CPU, cache is beside it, RAM is near it, the disk is far from it, tape is in a cupboard.' Distance from the CPU is exactly the order of speed and exactly the reverse order of capacity — so any question asking fastest, slowest, costliest per bit, or largest is answered by placing the item on that one line, not by recalling a separate fact.

RAM vs ROM by the letters: R-A-M = Random Access Memory = Read And Modify = volatile and temporary. R-O-M = Read Only Memory = Retains On Motionless (no power) = non-volatile and permanent. BIOS sits in ROM, which is why the machine can start before anything is loaded into RAM.

SRAM vs DRAM: the S is for Static — it stays put, no refresh, built from flip-flops, fast, expensive, small, so it is used as CACHE. The D is for Dynamic — it dies unless dynamically refreshed, built from capacitors, cheaper and denser, so it is used as MAIN MEMORY. One line to remember: 'Static sits in cache, Dynamic drives main memory.'

ROM family as an erasing ladder — each step erases more easily: MROM (masked, fixed at the factory, never erasable) → PROM (Programmable once by the user, then permanent) → EPROM (Erasable, but only by Ultra-Violet light, whole chip at once) → EEPROM (Electrically Erasable, byte by byte, no UV lamp needed). Flash memory is a form of EEPROM — that is why pen drives and SSDs are non-volatile.

Generations mnemonic: 'Vacuum Transistors Integrated Micro Artificial' — Vacuum tubes (1st), Transistors (2nd), Integrated Circuits (3rd), Microprocessors/VLSI (4th), Artificial Intelligence/ULSI and parallel processing (5th). Count on five fingers; the finger number is the generation number.

Storage ladder: FROM BYTE UPWARD every rung is ×1024 (2^10), never ×1000. Below byte it is different — 1 nibble = 4 bits, 1 byte = 8 bits = 2 nibbles. Chant the ladder 'bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB, EB, ZB, YB' and answer '1 PB = ?' by counting one rung down to TB, giving 1024 TB.

Binary↔Hex is grouping by 4 (because 2^4 = 16); binary↔Octal is grouping by 3 (because 2^3 = 8). Always group from the RIGHT and pad the left with zeros. So hex 2F → 0010 1111, and octal 27 → 010 111. Never convert via decimal in the exam; grouping is a two-second operation and decimal is a twenty-second one.

MICR is the bank-specific one and it is worth extra attention: Magnetic Ink Character Recognition, used on the bottom band of a cheque, 9-digit MICR code (3 city + 3 bank + 3 branch). OMR reads marks (OMR sheets in exams), OCR reads printed/typed characters, a barcode reader reads bars. Four different readers, four different jobs.

Printers split cleanly: IMPACT printers physically strike the paper (dot-matrix, daisy-wheel, line printer) and can therefore make carbon copies; NON-IMPACT do not touch it (inkjet, laser, thermal) and are quieter and faster. If a question mentions carbon copies or noise, it is asking about impact printers.
traps: RAM vs ROM vs Cache vs Register — all four are 'memory' and IBPS rotates which one it wants. Register = smallest and fastest, inside the CPU; Cache = between CPU and RAM, made of SRAM; RAM = main/primary memory, volatile; ROM = permanent, holds BIOS. A question asking 'fastest memory' wants Register; 'fastest between CPU and main memory' wants Cache. Read which one is asked.

Primary vs Secondary memory — an SSD is fast, so candidates classify it as primary. It is SECONDARY storage. Primary memory means only RAM, ROM and cache — the memory the CPU can address directly. Hard disk, SSD, pen drive, CD/DVD and tape are all secondary regardless of speed.

Volatile vs non-volatile — RAM is volatile (contents lost on power-off). Everything else in the standard list is non-volatile: ROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, flash, SSD, HDD, optical, tape. If the option set contains exactly one RAM variant, the volatile answer is that one.

SRAM vs DRAM reversed — the commonest single error in this module. SRAM is faster, costlier, needs NO refresh, and is used in cache. DRAM is slower, cheaper, NEEDS periodic refresh, and is used as main memory. Candidates who remember only 'D for Dynamic is faster' lose the mark.

EPROM vs EEPROM — EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light and only in full; EEPROM is erased electrically and can be done byte-wise. If the question says 'UV light', the answer is EPROM, not EEPROM. If it says 'electrically erasable' or 'without removing from the circuit', it is EEPROM.
1 KB = 1024 bytes, not 1000. The five-option format almost always plants 1000 as a decoy alongside 1024. The same trap runs the whole ladder: 1 TB = 1024 GB, 1 PB = 1024 TB.

Generation-to-technology mismatch — 3rd generation is Integrated Circuits and 4th is Microprocessors/VLSI. Candidates who compress the middle two generations put transistors in the 3rd. Transistors are 2nd generation only.

Input vs output vs both — plotter and projector are OUTPUT only; scanner, joystick, light pen, barcode reader and microphone are INPUT only; touchscreen, modem, NIC, hard disk and headset are BOTH. The question 'which is not an input device' usually hides a plotter or a printer among four genuine input devices.

Compiler vs Interpreter vs Assembler — compiler translates the whole high-level program at once and reports all errors together; interpreter translates and executes line by line, stopping at the first error; assembler converts assembly language to machine code. These three get swapped constantly.

System vs Application vs Utility software, and firmware vs freeware vs shareware — an operating system, device driver and compiler are SYSTEM software; MS-Word and a browser are APPLICATION software; antivirus and disk-defragmenter are UTILITY software. Firmware is software stored permanently in ROM (BIOS) and has nothing to do with freeware (free of cost) or shareware (free trial, then pay).
Number-base direction — grouping by 3 is octal and by 4 is hexadecimal, and candidates under time pressure reverse them. Anchor it on the base: 8 = 2^3 so three bits; 16 = 2^4 so four bits.
comp-fundamentals.timeTarget: 10-15 seconds per question, from reading the stem to marking the option. A pure-recall computer question that takes you more than 20 seconds is a question you do not know — mark it for review, move on, and do not guess into 0.25 negative. Across the ~5 computer questions in the section your entire budget is 60-75 seconds, so that the remaining 34 minutes belong to the puzzles and seating arrangements.
comp-fundamentals.masteryCheck: You can recite all ten boxes of the revision sheet aloud, from folded headings only, in under 6 minutes with zero prompts — including the full ROM ladder with its erasing method and the full storage ladder. And: given a 25-question mixed set from previous-year Clerk/PO Mains papers with five options each and a 15-second-per-question timer, you score at least 23 correct with at most 1 attempted-and-wrong. Attempting fewer and leaving the rest blank counts as a pass; guessing into a wrong answer does not.
questionPatterns: Which of the following memories is volatile in nature? (a) ROM (b) PROM (c) RAM (d) EPROM (e) Flash memory. — Answer: (c) RAM. It loses its contents the moment power is removed; every other option is non-volatile. This is the single most repeated computer question in Clerk Mains.

Which type of RAM does not need to be refreshed periodically? (a) DRAM (b) SDRAM (c) SRAM (d) DDR-RAM (e) RD-RAM. — Answer: (c) SRAM. It is built from flip-flops and holds its value as long as power is supplied, which is why it is used for cache; all the DRAM variants listed need constant refreshing.

The third generation of computers is characterised by the use of which technology? (a) Vacuum tubes (b) Transistors (c) Integrated Circuits (d) Microprocessors (e) Artificial Intelligence. — Answer: (c) Integrated Circuits. Vacuum tubes are 1st, transistors 2nd, microprocessors/VLSI 4th, AI/ULSI 5th.

1 Petabyte is equal to — (a) 1024 Gigabytes (b) 1024 Terabytes (c) 1000 Terabytes (d) 1024 Megabytes (e) 1024 Exabytes. — Answer: (b) 1024 Terabytes. Note that (c) is the decimal decoy and (e) inverts the ladder.

The binary equivalent of the hexadecimal number 2F is — (a) 00101111 (b) 00111111 (c) 01001111 (d) 00101011 (e) 11110010. — Answer: (a) 00101111. Each hex digit becomes exactly four bits: 2 = 0010 and F = 1111.

Which device is used by banks to read the characters printed at the bottom of a cheque? (a) OMR (b) OCR (c) MICR (d) Barcode reader (e) Light pen. — Answer: (c) MICR, Magnetic Ink Character Recognition. OMR reads pencil marks on answer sheets, OCR reads ordinary printed text.

Which of the following is the fastest memory in a computer system? (a) Cache memory (b) Main memory (c) Register (d) Magnetic disk (e) Magnetic tape. — Answer: (c) Register. It sits inside the CPU itself; cache is the correct answer only when the question specifically asks what lies between the CPU and main memory.

Which of the following is NOT an input device? (a) Scanner (b) Joystick (c) Light pen (d) Plotter (e) Microphone. — Answer: (d) Plotter, which is an output device used to draw large-format graphics and maps.

EPROM can be erased by — (a) electrical signals (b) ultraviolet light (c) infrared light (d) high temperature (e) it cannot be erased at all. — Answer: (b) ultraviolet light. Electrical erasing describes EEPROM, and (e) describes PROM.

Which of the following is an example of system software? (a) MS-Excel (b) Google Chrome (c) Operating system (d) Tally (e) Adobe Photoshop. — Answer: (c) Operating system. All the others are application software.

comp-fundamentals.aiPrompt: Act as an IBPS Clerk Mains paper setter for the Reasoning Ability & Computer Aptitude section. Generate 15 Computer Awareness MCQs on computer fundamentals — hardware vs software, input/output devices, CPU units, memory hierarchy, RAM vs ROM types (DRAM/SRAM, PROM/EPROM/EEPROM), generations of computers, storage units, number-system conversion, types of computers. Every question must have EXACTLY FIVE options labelled (a) to (e) with exactly one correct answer — never five options. Match real IBPS Clerk Mains difficulty: one-line stems, no scenario paragraphs. Deliberately build the wrong options out of the classic confusion pairs (SRAM vs DRAM, EPROM vs EEPROM, register vs cache, 1024 vs 1000, 2nd vs 3rd generation, input vs output devices). Do not include any question whose answer depends on a specific software or hardware version. After all 15 questions, print an answer key where each entry gives the correct option, a one-line reason, and — for every distractor that is a known confusion — one line saying precisely why it is wrong. Finally, list which of my confusion pairs I should re-drill if I miss each question. I will answer each in under 15 seconds, so keep the stems short.
comp-fundamentals.blockPlan: Total build time 6-7 hours spread over the first two weeks, then maintenance only. Week 1: two 45-minute blocks to build the A4 sheet by hand from the book (Day 1 = side 1, hardware and memory; Day 2 = side 2, units, number systems, computer types). One 30-minute block for the binary/octal/hex drill. Days 3 and 7 get a 10-minute recitation slot appended to the end of an existing Reasoning session — never given its own study block, because a recall module should ride on other work, not compete with it. Week 2 onwards: a 25-question timed set every Wednesday and Saturday inside the 15-minute buffer after your Reasoning practice, plus a 6-minute recitation on Days 14 and 30. From month two to exam: one fortnightly 6-minute recitation and one weekly 25-question set. Total ongoing cost about 25 minutes a week. In the final week, 6 minutes daily, no new facts.

comp-os.topicName: Operating Systems and MS Office — Windows, Word, Excel, PowerPoint
comp-os.whatItIs: The 'software you actually use' block: what an operating system does and its types, Windows file management and keyboard shortcuts, and the three MS Office applications IBPS asks about — Word (formatting, mail merge, track changes), Excel (cell references, the standard function set, charts) and PowerPoint (views, transitions, slide show keys) — plus the file-extension table. This is the second-largest computer slice in Clerk Mains, usually 1-2 of the 5 questions, and it is the friendliest, because you have used most of it. Note the version position as of this exam cycle: Windows 11 is the current consumer Windows (Windows 10 support ended 14 October 2025; the current servicing versions are 25H2 and 26H2, and there is no Windows 12). Office 2024 is the current perpetual standalone release, with Microsoft 365 as the subscription line. IBPS almost never asks a version-specific question, but it does assume the Office 2007-onward extensions (.docx / .xlsx / .pptx).
comp-os.coreMethod:
1. One A4 revision sheet again, but structured as four TABLES rather than boxes, because everything in this module is naturally tabular and tables are what your memory will reconstruct under pressure.
2. Table 1 — OS: left column the six functions (process, memory, file, device, security, user interface); right column the types with one distinguishing phrase each (batch = jobs grouped, no user interaction; multiprogramming = several programs in memory; multitasking = one user, several tasks; multiprocessing = several CPUs; time-sharing = many users, CPU time slice/quantum each; distributed = many machines look like one; real-time = strict deadline, hard vs soft; embedded/mobile = fixed-purpose device). Add the examples row: Windows, Linux (open source), Unix (multi-user), macOS, Android, iOS, DOS (single-user, single-tasking, CLI).
3. Table 2 — Shortcuts, in three columns: universal Ctrl combinations, function keys F1-F12, and Windows-key combinations. Write only the ones IBPS actually asks; a shortcut list of 200 items is a list you will never recall.
4. Table 3 — Office, one row per application: Word (tabs and what lives on each, mail merge, track changes, key shortcuts), Excel (workbook/worksheet/cell, reference types, the eight functions, chart-to-purpose mapping), PowerPoint (views, transition vs animation, slide-show keys).
5. Table 4 — Extensions, grouped by owner: Office (.docx .dotx .docm .xlsx .xlsm .csv .pptx .ppsx .potx .accdb), system (.exe .sys .dll .bat), media (.jpg .png .gif .mp3 .wav .mp4 .mkv), other (.pdf .txt .zip .rar .html).
6. Hands-on beats reading for this one module only. Spend one 40-minute session at an actual computer doing five things once each: run a mail merge, switch a formula between A1 / $A$1 / $A1 using F4, write an IF and a VLOOKUP, apply and then accept a tracked change, and run a slide show with a transition and an animation on the same slide. Physically doing each once fixes it better than ten readings, and it permanently separates the pairs IBPS exploits.
7. Self-test protocol: cover the right-hand column of each table and reconstruct it aloud. For shortcuts, test in the harder direction — given the ACTION, produce the key combination, not the reverse. Exams ask both, and the action→key direction is the one that fails.
8. Spaced revision: Day 0 build, then Days 1, 3, 7, 14, 30, then fortnightly. Six minutes each after Day 7.
9. Twice-weekly 25-question timed set from previous-year papers at 15 seconds per question, with the same error-log discipline as the fundamentals module: log the confused PAIR, not the question.
10. Final week: recite the four tables daily. Do not learn new shortcuts in the last ten days — a half-learned shortcut is worse than an unknown one because it produces a confident wrong answer at 0.25 negative.
tricks: Time-sharing vs multiprogramming vs multitasking, settled by counting users and CPUs: multiprogramming = several programs sitting in memory so the CPU is never idle; multitasking = ONE user running several tasks; time-sharing = MANY users, each given a fixed time slice (quantum) so each thinks the machine is his alone; multiprocessing = several CPUs/processors in one system. The keyword 'time slice' or 'quantum' always means time-sharing; the keyword 'more than one processor' always means multiprocessing.

Excel references and the dollar sign: $ means 'freeze whatever comes immediately after me'. $A$1 freezes both column and row — absolute, never changes when copied. A$1 freezes only the row, $A1 only the column — mixed. A1 with no dollars is relative and shifts in both directions. F4 cycles A1 → $A$1 → A$1 → $A1 → A1, which is also the fastest way to check yourself in the exam if you can picture the cycle.

COUNT family disambiguated in one line: COUNT counts numbers only; COUNTA counts Anything non-empty (text included); COUNTBLANK counts empty cells; COUNTIF counts only what matches a condition. 'A' stands for All-that-is-there. A question that shows a range with text and numbers is testing exactly this distinction.

VLOOKUP: V is for Vertical, so it searches DOWN the first column of the table and returns a value from a column to the right. Syntax VLOOKUP(lookup_value, table_array, col_index_num, [range_lookup]) — four arguments, and the fourth is FALSE (or 0) for an exact match, TRUE for approximate. HLOOKUP is the Horizontal twin that searches across the first row. Remember 'V looks down, H looks across'.

Transition vs Animation in PowerPoint: a TRANSITION happens BETWEEN two slides (it transports you from one slide to the next); an ANIMATION happens WITHIN one slide, to text or an object on it. Both words start with the letter of what they act on if you phrase it as 'Transition = To the next slide, Animation = An object'.

PowerPoint slide-show keys: F5 starts from the FIRST slide; Shift+F5 starts from the CURRENT slide (Shift means 'shift the start to where I am'); Esc ends the show; during a show, B blanks the screen Black and W blanks it White.

Function-key meaning depends on the application, so anchor each to its home: F1 = Help (everywhere), F2 = Rename (Windows) / edit cell (Excel), F5 = Refresh (Windows/browser) / Go To (Excel) / start slide show (PowerPoint), F7 = spell check (Office), F12 = Save As (Office). If a question does not name the application, it is asking about the Windows meaning.

Save vs Save As, in one rule: Save (Ctrl+S) overwrites the existing file; Save As (F12) creates a new copy with a new name, location or format. The first time you ever save a new file, Save behaves like Save As because there is nothing to overwrite — which is exactly the case IBPS words as a trick stem.

Delete vs Shift+Delete: Delete sends the file to the Recycle Bin, from where it can be restored; Shift+Delete bypasses the Recycle Bin and removes it permanently. Files deleted from a pen drive or network drive also bypass the Recycle Bin. 'Shift means skip the bin.'

Chart-to-purpose mapping, four items only: PIE for parts of a whole (percentages of one total), LINE for a trend over time, BAR/COLUMN for comparing separate categories, SCATTER (XY) for the relationship between two variables. A question that says 'contribution of each branch to total deposits' wants pie; 'growth over five years' wants line.
traps: Multitasking vs multiprogramming vs time-sharing vs multiprocessing — four similar words, and the option set will contain at least three of them. Match on the keyword: time slice → time-sharing, one user many tasks → multitasking, many programs in memory → multiprogramming, many CPUs → multiprocessing.

Real-time hard vs soft, and real-time vs batch — a real-time OS has a strict deadline (missile guidance, pacemaker = hard; live streaming = soft). A batch OS groups jobs with no user interaction and is the opposite of interactive. Payroll processing overnight = batch, not real-time.
COUNT vs COUNTA vs COUNTIF — described above; this is the single most-missed Excel question, because candidates remember COUNT as 'counts cells' rather than 'counts numeric cells'.

Relative vs absolute vs mixed reference — the trap is a stem that says 'does not change when the formula is copied' while placing $A1 and A$1 in the options alongside $A$1. Only $A$1 is fully unchanged; the mixed forms change in one direction.
Transition vs animation — reversed by roughly half of all candidates. Transition is between slides, animation is within a slide.
Recycle Bin behaviour — candidates assume everything deleted is recoverable. Shift+Delete, deletions from removable/pen drives, and files larger than the Recycle Bin allocation are all permanent.
F5 across applications — Refresh in Windows and browsers, Go To in Excel, Start Slide Show in PowerPoint. If the question names PowerPoint, 'refresh' is a wasted mark.
Cut vs Copy — Cut (Ctrl+X) removes from the source, Copy (Ctrl+C) leaves it. Combined with the Clipboard, a question may ask what remains at the original location after each.

File extensions confused within the same family — .docx is a Word document, .dotx a Word template, .docm a macro-enabled document; likewise .xlsx / .xltx / .xlsm and .pptx (presentation) / .ppsx (slide show that opens straight into the show) / .potx (template). Also .accdb is Access 2007 onward while .mdb is the older Access format.

Word tab locations — Mail Merge is on the MAILINGS tab, Track Changes and Spelling & Grammar and Word Count on the REVIEW tab, Header/Footer and Page Number and Table on the INSERT tab, Margins and Orientation and Columns on the LAYOUT tab. Candidates place mail merge under Insert or Review and lose the mark.
Ctrl+Z vs Ctrl+Y — Z undoes, Y redoes. Reversing them is a pure carelessness loss under time pressure.

Operating system classification — an OS is system software, never application software, and Linux is open source while Unix historically is not. DOS is single-user AND single-tasking, which is a two-part fact that gets half-remembered.
comp-os.timeTarget: 10-15 seconds. Shortcut and extension questions should be near-instant — under 8 seconds — because they are single-fact lookups. An Excel question that shows a small data range may take up to 20 seconds; that is the ceiling. Total budget for the 1-2 Office questions in the paper is about 25 seconds.
comp-os.masteryCheck: You can reproduce all four tables from covered headings in under 7 minutes, and you can answer the action→key direction (given 'permanently delete a file without sending it to the Recycle Bin', you say Shift+Delete) for 20 out of 20 shortcuts without hesitation. Plus: on a 25-question timed Office/OS set with five options each at 15 seconds per question, at least 22 correct with no more than 1 wrong attempt. Separately, you must be able to state, without looking, what each of the four VLOOKUP arguments does and what the fourth one must be for an exact match.
questionPatterns: In MS-Excel, which of the following is an absolute cell reference that does not change when the formula is copied to another cell? (a) A1 (b) $A1 (c) A$1 (d) $A$1 (e) A:1. — Answer: (d) $A$1. Options (b) and (c) are mixed references that stay fixed in only one direction.

Which Excel function counts only those cells in a range that contain numbers? (a) COUNTA (b) COUNT (c) COUNTIF (d) COUNTBLANK (e) SUM. — Answer: (b) COUNT. COUNTA would also count text entries, which is the intended trap.

In MS-PowerPoint, which key is used to start the slide show from the very first slide? (a) F2 (b) F5 (c) Shift+F5 (d) F7 (e) Ctrl+F5. — Answer: (b) F5. Shift+F5 starts from the current slide, and F7 runs the spell check.

Which key combination opens Task Manager directly in Windows? (a) Ctrl+Alt+Delete (b) Ctrl+Shift+Esc (c) Alt+F4 (d) Windows+R (e) Ctrl+Esc. — Answer: (b) Ctrl+Shift+Esc. Ctrl+Alt+Delete opens the security options screen from which Task Manager must then be chosen.

An operating system in which the CPU's time is divided among several users by allotting each a fixed time slice is called — (a) Batch operating system (b) Real-time operating system (c) Time-sharing operating system (d) Distributed operating system (e) Embedded operating system. — Answer: (c) Time-sharing. The words 'time slice' and 'quantum' are the giveaway.
The Mail Merge feature in MS-Word is available under which tab? (a) Insert (b) Review (c) References (d) Mailings (e) Layout. — Answer: (d) Mailings.

Which of the following is the default file extension of a presentation created in MS-PowerPoint 2007 and later? (a) .ppt (b) .pptx (c) .ppsx (d) .potx (e) .pps. — Answer: (b) .pptx. The .ppsx format opens directly into the slide show and .potx is a template.
Track Changes in MS-Word is found on which tab? (a) Home (b) Insert (c) Review (d) View (e) Layout. — Answer: (c) Review, along with Spelling & Grammar, Word Count and Comments.
Which of the following permanently deletes a file without sending it to the Recycle Bin? (a) Delete (b) Ctrl+Delete (c) Shift+Delete (d) Alt+Delete (e) Ctrl+Shift+D. — Answer: (c) Shift+Delete.

In MS-Excel, the VLOOKUP function searches for a value in the — (a) last column of the table (b) first row of the table (c) first column of the table (d) last row of the table (e) entire worksheet. — Answer: (c) first column of the table. Searching the first ROW is HLOOKUP, which is the planted confusion.

comp-network.topicName: Networking and Internet — LAN/WAN, Topologies, OSI Layers, Protocols, IP and E-mail
comp-network.whatItIs: Everything about machines talking to each other: network types by geographic range (PAN/LAN/MAN/WAN), the five topologies and their trade-offs, the seven OSI layers in order with the device that operates at each, the protocol table (TCP/IP, HTTP/HTTPS, FTP, SMTP, POP3, IMAP, DNS, DHCP) with what each one actually does and its port, IPv4 vs IPv6 addressing, URL anatomy, browsers and search engines, e-mail terminology including CC vs BCC, transmission modes, connection types, and basic internet security terms. Usually 1-2 of the 5 computer questions, and for a banking exam it earns its keep twice over, since the same protocol and security vocabulary reappears in General Awareness through digital-banking questions. Version note for this cycle: HTTP/3 over QUIC and TLS 1.3 are now mainstream on the web, and Wi-Fi 7 (IEEE 802.11be) was finalised in July 2025 — but IBPS Clerk questions stay on the stable core (HTTP/HTTPS, ports, OSI, IPv4/IPv6), so learn the core cold and treat the newer names as recognition-only.
comp-network.coreMethod:
1. One A4 sheet, five zones, laid out spatially so recall has a map.
2. Zone A — the range ladder, drawn as one line with distances marked: PAN (~10 m, Bluetooth) → LAN (a building or campus, up to ~1-2 km, privately owned, highest speed, cheapest per node) → CAN (a campus) → MAN (a city, roughly 5-50 km, connects LANs, e.g. a cable TV network) → WAN (a country or the globe, unlimited range, slowest per link, the Internet is the largest WAN). Write speed and cost as arrows along the same line — as range grows, speed falls and error rate rises.
3. Zone B — topologies as five small drawings, not words. Under each write one advantage and one weakness in four words: Bus (cheapest, least cable / backbone fails = whole network down, needs terminators); Star (easy to add or remove a node, one node's failure harms nobody / central hub or switch fails = all down, most common LAN layout today); Ring (each node connects to exactly two, token passing, no collisions / a single break can halt the ring); Mesh (every node linked to every other, n(n-1)/2 links in a full mesh, most fault-tolerant / most expensive, most cabling); Tree (hierarchical, star-of-buses, easy expansion / depends on the root).
4. Zone C — OSI as a seven-rung ladder written BOTTOM-UP, with three columns: layer name, its data unit, its device/function. Physical (bits; hub, repeater, cables) → Data Link (frames; switch, bridge, NIC, MAC addressing, error detection) → Network (packets; router, IP addressing and routing) → Transport (segments; TCP/UDP, end-to-end delivery, flow control) → Session (dialogue control, establishing and ending sessions) → Presentation (translation, encryption, compression) → Application (user services; HTTP, FTP, SMTP, DNS). Next to it write the 4-layer TCP/IP model: Network Access, Internet, Transport, Application.
5. Zone D — the protocol table, one row per protocol: name, expansion, one-line job, port. This table is the single highest-yield object in the module; roughly a third of all networking questions come straight out of it.
6. Zone E — internet and e-mail miscellany: URL anatomy dissected on one worked example, TLD list, browsers vs search engines, To/CC/BCC, transmission modes, connection types, and a six-item security strip (virus, worm, Trojan, ransomware, spyware, phishing) with one line each.
7. Self-test: for OSI, recite bottom-up AND top-down, plus the device at each layer — exams ask 'which layer does a router work at' far more often than they ask for the list. For protocols, cover the port column and reconstruct it, then cover the job column and reconstruct that.
8. Spaced revision: Day 0 build, Days 1, 3, 7, 14, 30, then fortnightly, 6 minutes each after Day 7.
9. Twice-weekly 25-question timed set at 15 seconds each, error log recording the confused PAIR.
10. Cross-link deliberately: whenever you revise the digital-banking part of General Awareness (UPI, NEFT, RTGS, IMPS, tokenisation, two-factor authentication), read Zone E's security strip at the same sitting. The two syllabi share vocabulary and revising them together halves the time. Verified figures worth knowing for that cross-link: RTGS has an RBI-set minimum of ₹2 lakh per transaction with no upper limit and runs 24x7x365; NEFT has no minimum and settles in half-hourly batches 24x7; IMPS runs up to ₹5 lakh depending on the bank; standard UPI is ₹1 lakh per day with higher caps for specified categories.
tricks: Range ladder by the letter that changes: Local (one building), Metropolitan (one metro/city), Wide (a country or the world). The word itself gives the scale, so no separate memorisation is needed — you only need the numbers: LAN up to about 1-2 km, MAN about 5-50 km, WAN beyond that.

OSI bottom-up mnemonic: 'Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away' — Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application. Top-down: 'All People Seem To Need Data Processing'. Always write which direction you memorised, because layer-number questions (layer 3 = Network) depend entirely on counting from the bottom.

Devices by layer, in one chain: 'Hub is dumb, Switch is smart, Router is smartest, Gateway translates.' Hub and repeater = Physical (layer 1); switch, bridge and NIC = Data Link (layer 2); router = Network (layer 3); gateway = works across all layers and connects two dissimilar networks. This chain answers more questions than the layer list does.

Mail protocols split by direction: SMTP has an S for Send (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, port 25). POP3 and IMAP both Pull mail down. The difference between the two: POP3 (port 110) DOWNLOADS mail to one device and typically removes it from the server; IMAP (port 143) keeps the mail ON the server and synchronises it across all your devices. 'POP takes it away, IMAP leaves it there.'

Port numbers worth having cold, as a short chant: FTP 20 and 21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP 25, DNS 53, HTTP 80, POP3 110, IMAP 143, HTTPS 443. Notice HTTPS 443 is the one most often asked, because the S-for-Secure adds TLS/SSL encryption.

IPv4 vs IPv6 by counting: IPv4 is 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers 0-255 separated by dots (192.168.1.1), giving about 4.3 billion addresses. IPv6 is 128 bits — four times the BIT LENGTH of IPv4's 32, which is not four times as many addresses but 2^96 times as many (about 3.4 x 10^38 in total against IPv4's 4.3 billion). Anchor it as '4 → 32 dotted decimal, 6 → 128 colon hex'. A MAC address is a third thing entirely: 48 bits, hexadecimal, burned into the NIC, a physical address not an internet address.

DNS vs DHCP, the two most-swapped acronyms: DNS = Domain Name System = translates a NAME into an IP address (it is the internet's phone book). DHCP = Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol = hands OUT an IP address to a device joining the network. 'DNS finds the address, DHCP gives you one.'

CC vs BCC: Carbon Copy — every recipient can see who else got it. Blind Carbon Copy — the addresses are hidden, so no recipient can see the BCC list. Remember 'B is for Blind, and blind means invisible to the others'.

Transmission modes by everyday objects: Simplex = one direction only (keyboard to computer, TV broadcast); Half-duplex = both directions but one at a time (walkie-talkie); Full-duplex = both directions simultaneously (telephone call). Exams almost always use exactly these three examples.

Virus vs worm vs Trojan, the three-line separation: a VIRUS attaches itself to a host file and needs the user to run that file before it spreads; a WORM is standalone and self-replicates across a network with no host file and no user action; a TROJAN disguises itself as legitimate software and does NOT self-replicate at all. 'Virus needs a host, worm needs nothing, Trojan needs your trust.'

URL anatomy on one worked example — in https://www.example.co.in/careers/apply.html the parts are: protocol (https), subdomain (www), domain name (example), top-level domain (.co / .in as country code), path (/careers), file name (apply.html). Learn it on one example and you can dissect any URL a question offers.
traps: LAN vs MAN vs WAN ranges — candidates know the words but not the numbers, and options are built from the numbers. LAN roughly up to 1-2 km within a building or campus, MAN roughly 5-50 km across a city, WAN beyond a city with no upper limit. Also: a MAN is made of interconnected LANs, and the Internet is a WAN, not a MAN.

Hub vs Switch vs Router vs Gateway, and their layers — a hub broadcasts to every port (layer 1), a switch forwards only to the intended port using MAC addresses (layer 2), a router forwards between different networks using IP addresses (layer 3), a gateway connects two dissimilar networks and works at all layers. 'Which device works at the network layer' is a standard question and the answer is router.

OSI layer order and layer numbering — Session and Presentation are routinely swapped. Session is layer 5, Presentation is layer 6. Encryption and compression happen at PRESENTATION, not at Session and not at Application.

TCP vs UDP — TCP is connection-oriented, reliable, acknowledges and re-sends lost data, and is slower; UDP is connectionless, unreliable, has no acknowledgement, and is faster, which is why it is used for streaming and voice calls. Candidates who remember only 'TCP/IP' as one word cannot answer the split.
DNS vs DHCP — the most-swapped acronym pair in the whole module. DNS resolves names to IP addresses; DHCP assigns IP addresses dynamically.

SMTP vs POP3 vs IMAP — SMTP only SENDS. If a question asks which protocol is used to RECEIVE or RETRIEVE mail, SMTP is wrong and the answer is POP3 or IMAP, distinguished by whether the mail stays on the server (IMAP) or is downloaded off it (POP3).
HTTP vs HTTPS — the S is Secure, meaning the traffic is encrypted with SSL/TLS; the ports are 80 and 443 respectively. A stem mentioning a padlock, secure transactions or net banking wants HTTPS.

IPv4 vs IPv6 bit counts — 32 and 128. The five-option format plants 64 and 256 as decoys, and also plants 48, which is the MAC address length, to catch candidates who blur physical and logical addressing.

Browser vs search engine — Google Chrome is a BROWSER, Google (google.com) is a SEARCH ENGINE, and the two are constantly conflated. Bing and DuckDuckGo are search engines; Firefox, Edge, Safari, Opera and Brave are browsers. Internet Explorer was retired in June 2022 and replaced by Edge.

Bus vs Ring failure behaviour — in a bus topology the failure of the main backbone cable brings the whole network down, but a single node failing does not; in a star topology a single node failing does not matter but the central hub failing kills everything. Questions test which single failure is fatal, so learn the weakness, not just the advantage.
Mesh link count — a fully connected mesh with n nodes has n(n-1)/2 links, not n(n-1). The unhalved figure counts each link twice and is always planted as an option.
CC vs BCC — the trap stem is 'which field hides the recipients from each other', where CC is the plausible-looking wrong answer.
Virus vs worm — a worm does not need a host file or any user action; a virus does. Stems saying 'spreads by itself across a network' mean worm, and stems saying 'attaches to a program' mean virus.
comp-network.timeTarget: 10-15 seconds. Port numbers, full forms and OSI-layer questions should land in under 10 seconds because they are single table lookups. Topology questions that describe a layout in a sentence may take 20 seconds; that is the ceiling. Budget about 25 seconds total for the 1-2 networking questions in the paper.
comp-network.masteryCheck: You can write out the seven OSI layers bottom-up with data unit and device for each in under 90 seconds, and the full protocol table with ports in under 2 minutes, both from a blank sheet. You can state the failure weakness (not just the advantage) of all five topologies. And on a 25-question timed networking set with five options each at 15 seconds per question, at least 22 correct with no more than 1 wrong attempt. If you cannot separate DNS from DHCP and POP3 from IMAP instantly, you have not passed regardless of the score.
questionPatterns: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for routing packets between different networks? (a) Data Link layer (b) Transport layer (c) Network layer (d) Session layer (e) Physical layer. — Answer: (c) Network layer, which is layer 3 and where a router operates.

An IPv6 address consists of how many bits? (a) 32 bits (b) 64 bits (c) 128 bits (d) 48 bits (e) 256 bits. — Answer: (c) 128 bits. IPv4 is 32 bits and 48 bits is the length of a MAC address, both planted as decoys.

Which protocol is used to SEND an e-mail from a client to a mail server? (a) POP3 (b) IMAP (c) SMTP (d) FTP (e) SNMP. — Answer: (c) SMTP, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, on port 25. POP3 and IMAP are used to retrieve mail, not send it.

In which network topology are all the devices connected to a single central device such as a hub or a switch? (a) Bus (b) Ring (c) Star (d) Mesh (e) Tree. — Answer: (c) Star. Its weakness is that failure of the central hub brings down the entire network.

Which of the following converts a domain name into its corresponding IP address? (a) DHCP (b) DNS (c) FTP (d) ARP (e) SMTP. — Answer: (b) DNS. DHCP is the decoy — it assigns IP addresses to devices rather than resolving names.
The default port number used by HTTPS is — (a) 21 (b) 25 (c) 80 (d) 443 (e) 110. — Answer: (d) 443. Port 80 is plain HTTP, 21 is FTP control, 25 is SMTP and 110 is POP3.

Which e-mail field allows you to send a copy of a message to a recipient without the other recipients knowing? (a) To (b) CC (c) BCC (d) Subject (e) Reply-All. — Answer: (c) BCC, Blind Carbon Copy. In CC every recipient can see the full list.

A telephone conversation, in which both parties can speak and listen at the same time, is an example of which transmission mode? (a) Simplex (b) Half-duplex (c) Full-duplex (d) Multiplex (e) Duplexing. — Answer: (c) Full-duplex. A walkie-talkie is half-duplex and a television broadcast is simplex.

Which of the following is a self-replicating malicious program that spreads across a network without needing to attach itself to a host file? (a) Virus (b) Worm (c) Trojan horse (d) Spyware (e) Adware. — Answer: (b) Worm. A virus requires a host file and user execution; a Trojan does not self-replicate at all.

Which of the following is a search engine and NOT a web browser? (a) Google Chrome (b) Mozilla Firefox (c) Microsoft Edge (d) Google (e) Safari. — Answer: (d) Google. Chrome is the browser made by Google, and the option pair is designed to exploit exactly that confusion.

comp-security.topicName: Computer Security, Malware and Cyber-Attack Terms
comp-security.whatItIs: The single most frequently asked Computer Awareness cluster in IBPS Clerk Mains. It covers the malware family (virus, worm, trojan, ransomware, spyware, adware, keylogger, botnet), social-engineering frauds (phishing, vishing, smishing, pharming), defensive tools (firewall, antivirus, encryption), the public-key ideas (symmetric vs asymmetric keys, digital signature, digital certificate), authentication factors and OTP, SSL/TLS and the browser padlock, hacker hat colours, and attack names (DoS, DDoS, man-in-the-middle, SQL injection, brute force). Nothing here is solved — it is recognised. A Mains computer question is a one-line definition asked backwards: the paper gives you the behaviour and five candidate terms, and you either own the definition or you leave it blank. Because these sit inside the Reasoning Ability & Computer Aptitude section at ~1.5 marks on average, a correct 12-second answer is the cheapest mark in the entire paper, and every second saved here goes to a puzzle set.
comp-security.coreMethod:
1. Build ONE A4 revision sheet, front and back, and never let it grow to two. Front page = six boxes. Back page = the attack-and-fraud vocabulary list. Handwrite it; typing it does not encode it.
2. BOX 1 — Malware, written as a table with three columns: NAME | NEEDS A HOST FILE? | SPREADS BY ITSELF? Rows: Virus (yes host / no self-spread, needs user to run the infected file), Worm (no host / yes self-spread across a network), Trojan (disguised as useful software, no self-replication, opens a backdoor), Ransomware (encrypts your files, demands payment, WannaCry is the stock example), Spyware (silently collects data), Keylogger (a spyware subtype recording keystrokes), Adware (forces advertisements), Rootkit (hides itself with admin-level access), Botnet/zombie (infected machines controlled remotely), Logic bomb (triggers on a condition or date). Writing the two yes/no columns is the whole point — that grid is what IBPS tests.
3. BOX 2 — Social engineering by CHANNEL: Phishing = fake email or fake website; Vishing = Voice call; Smishing = SMS; Pharming = you type the correct address but DNS poisoning redirects you to a fake site; Spear phishing = phishing aimed at one named individual; Whaling = aimed at a senior executive; Shoulder surfing = watching you enter a PIN; Skimming = copying card data at an ATM or POS.
4. BOX 3 — Cryptography, four lines only: Symmetric = ONE shared key, fast, examples DES/3DES/AES; Asymmetric = key PAIR, examples RSA/ECC; for CONFIDENTIALITY encrypt with the receiver's PUBLIC key and the receiver decrypts with their private key; for AUTHENTICITY the sender signs with their OWN PRIVATE key and anyone verifies with the sender's public key. Then two lines: Digital signature = made by the sender using their private key, gives authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation; Digital certificate = issued by a Certifying Authority, binds a public key to an identity, X.509 is the standard.
5. BOX 4 — Defences: Firewall = filters traffic entering or leaving a network, hardware or software, works at the boundary; Antivirus = scans files already on the machine, detects by signature and heuristics, must be updated; Proxy server = intermediary that hides the internal address; VPN = encrypted tunnel over a public network; Sandbox = isolated test area; Patch = security fix. One line: a firewall does NOT remove an existing virus, and an antivirus does NOT filter network traffic.
6. BOX 5 — Authentication: the three factors are Something you KNOW (password, PIN), something you HAVE (OTP, token, card, mobile), something you ARE (fingerprint, iris, face). Two-factor authentication needs two DIFFERENT factors. OTP is time-limited and single-use and belongs to the HAVE factor. Add: authentication = proving who you are; authorisation = what you are then allowed to do.
7. BOX 6 — Web security: SSL is the obsolete predecessor; TLS is the current protocol and TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446, 2018) is the current version, with all SSL versions and TLS 1.0/1.1 deprecated. HTTPS = HTTP over TLS, port 443 (HTTP is port 80). The padlock means only that the connection is encrypted and the certificate is valid — it does NOT certify that the site is genuine or honest; criminals buy certificates too. Add Wi-Fi security order WEP (weakest, broken) < WPA < WPA2 < WPA3 (current).
8. BACK PAGE — attack and actor vocabulary, one line each: DoS (one source floods a server), DDoS (many compromised machines, a botnet, flood it), Man-in-the-Middle (attacker silently sits between two parties), SQL injection (malicious SQL entered into an input box to reach the database), Brute force (tries every combination), Dictionary attack (tries a wordlist), Zero-day (flaw with no patch yet), Cookie (a small text file, NOT malware), Spoofing (faking an identity or address), Spam, Cyber-stalking, Salami attack (many tiny thefts), Ethical hacking. Hat colours: White = tests with permission, Black = criminal, Grey = no permission but no criminal intent, plus Script kiddie = unskilled user of ready-made tools.
9. REVISION SCHEDULE, non-negotiable: read the sheet on Day 0, Day 1, Day 3, Day 7, Day 15, Day 30, then once a week until the exam. Each pass is 6-8 minutes, not 30.
10. SELF-TEST BY REVERSAL: cover the NAME column and read only the definition, then say the term aloud. Recognition of the name is worthless; the exam gives the definition. Do it in the other direction too, once a week.
11. ERROR LOG: keep a strip of paper at the bottom of the sheet listing only the terms you got wrong. Before the exam you revise that strip, not the sheet.
12. TIMED DRILL every Sunday: 30 terms, stopwatch, 8 minutes. Any term taking over 15 seconds goes onto the error strip even if you got it right.
tricks: HOST-AND-SPREAD test, the one device that settles the whole malware section: a VIRUS is a Vehicle passenger — it needs a host file to ride in and a user to start it; a WORM Wanders on its own — no host, no user, spreads across the network by itself; a TROJAN is a Trick — a disguise with no replication at all. If the question says 'spreads without user intervention', it is a worm, never a virus.

CHANNEL LETTERS for fraud: Vishing starts with V for Voice call; Smishing starts with S for SMS; Phishing is the general email/fake-website parent. Pharming has an R in it for Redirect — you typed the right address and DNS sent you to the wrong site.

KEY DIRECTION rule, said as five words: 'PUBLIC to Protect, PRIVATE to Prove.' To keep a message secret you encrypt with the RECEIVER's public key (protect); to prove you wrote it you sign with YOUR OWN private key (prove). This single line answers every asymmetric-key question the exam sets.

SIGNATURE vs CERTIFICATE: a signature is something you MAKE (with your private key); a certificate is something you are GIVEN (by a Certifying Authority). You cannot issue yourself a valid certificate, and a CA does not sign your document.

EXTRA D = DISTRIBUTED: DoS is one attacker machine; DDoS has an extra D because the traffic is distributed across many hijacked computers (a botnet). If the option mentions 'multiple compromised systems' or 'botnet', the answer is DDoS.

BORDER vs INTERIOR: a firewall guards the border (traffic in and out); an antivirus patrols the interior (files already on the disk). A question about 'unauthorised access to a network' is firewall; 'detect and remove malicious programs' is antivirus.

FACTOR TRIPLET, three words: KNOW, HAVE, ARE. Password = know, OTP/card/phone = have, fingerprint/iris/face = are. Two-factor means two different words from that list — a password plus a security question is still ONE factor, both are 'know'.

HAT COLOURS by permission: White has written permission, Black has criminal intent, Grey has neither permission nor criminal intent. Ask 'did the owner authorise it?' first, 'was harm intended?' second.

PADLOCK SENTENCE, memorise it verbatim: 'The padlock certifies the pipe, not the person.' It means the traffic is encrypted with a valid certificate; it says nothing about whether the website is honest.
LADDER for Wi-Fi and web protocols: WEP → WPA → WPA2 → WPA3 and SSL → TLS 1.0 → 1.1 → 1.2 → 1.3. In both ladders the last rung is the current one and everything to its left is deprecated.
traps: VIRUS vs WORM: the exam repeatedly describes a self-replicating program that spreads over a network with no user action and offers 'virus' as the tempting first option. That is a WORM. A virus requires a host file and requires the user to execute it.

WORM vs TROJAN: both are non-virus malware, but a Trojan does NOT self-replicate — it disguises itself as legitimate software and typically installs a backdoor. Any option describing 'appears useful but is harmful' is Trojan; 'copies itself repeatedly' is worm.

SPYWARE vs ADWARE vs RANSOMWARE: spyware watches and reports silently, adware forces advertisements, ransomware ENCRYPTS your data and demands payment. Scareware only pretends to have found an infection — it does not encrypt anything.

PHISHING vs VISHING vs SMISHING vs PHARMING: all four are the same fraud on different channels, and IBPS will place three of them in the same five options. Fix the channel word (email/web, voice, SMS, DNS redirect) before reading the options.

SYMMETRIC vs ASYMMETRIC: symmetric uses ONE key for both encryption and decryption (the key-distribution problem is its weakness); asymmetric uses a mathematically linked pair. AES/DES are symmetric; RSA is asymmetric. Candidates routinely tag RSA as symmetric because it is famous.

PUBLIC vs PRIVATE KEY DIRECTION: the most-missed question in the whole topic. Confidentiality uses the RECEIVER's public key. Signing uses the SENDER's private key. A private key is never shared, never transmitted and never used to encrypt a message for someone else's eyes only.

DIGITAL SIGNATURE vs DIGITAL CERTIFICATE vs ELECTRONIC SIGNATURE: the signature is generated by the sender's private key; the certificate is issued by a Certifying Authority and binds a public key to an identity; a scanned image of your handwritten signature is merely an electronic signature and is not a digital signature.

FIREWALL vs ANTIVIRUS: a firewall cannot remove a virus already sitting on your hard disk, and an antivirus cannot block unauthorised inbound network traffic. Questions are written specifically to catch candidates who treat them as synonyms.

AUTHENTICATION vs AUTHORISATION: authentication verifies identity (login, OTP, biometric); authorisation decides what that verified identity may access. Both start with 'auth' and both appear in the same option set.

SSL vs TLS: SSL is the older, deprecated protocol; TLS replaced it and TLS 1.3 is current. The phrase 'SSL certificate' survives in everyday use, which makes candidates answer SSL when the question asks for the protocol in current use — that is TLS.

PADLOCK MEANING: the padlock and HTTPS indicate an encrypted connection with a valid certificate. They do NOT mean the website is legitimate, safe or trustworthy. An option saying 'the website is genuine and safe' is deliberately planted and is wrong.
ENCRYPTION vs HASHING: encryption is two-way and reversible with a key; hashing (MD5, SHA) is one-way and cannot be reversed. Passwords are stored hashed, not encrypted.

COOKIE vs SPYWARE: a cookie is a small text file a website stores to remember your session or preferences. It is not a program, cannot execute and is not malware — but it appears as an option in malware questions.
DoS vs DDoS: one source versus many. Also note neither steals data — they deny availability. An option claiming a DoS attack 'steals confidential information' is wrong.

BRUTE FORCE vs DICTIONARY ATTACK: brute force tries every possible character combination; a dictionary attack tries a prepared list of likely words and leaked passwords. They are separate options in the same question.
HACKER HAT COLOURS: grey hat is not 'partly criminal' — it means acting without authorisation but without malicious intent. White hat is defined by having permission, not by skill level.
comp-security.timeTarget: 10-15 seconds per question, decision made on the first read. Recall should be instant: read the stem, name the term in your head BEFORE looking at the five options, then find it. If the term does not surface within 15 seconds it will not surface at 40 seconds either — leave it blank and move to the puzzle set, because at 0.25 negative a guess between five options is a losing bet. Target for a 5-question computer block inside the 35-minute section: 60-75 seconds total, leaving 33-plus minutes for reasoning.
comp-security.masteryCheck: You have mastered this module when, from a blank sheet and a stopwatch, you can (a) reproduce the malware grid — ten names with their host and self-spread columns — in under 4 minutes with no errors; (b) state the four key-direction facts (encrypt for secrecy, decrypt, sign, verify) correctly in under 20 seconds when asked in random order; (c) answer 30 mixed definition-to-term prompts in 8 minutes with at least 28 correct and no single item taking over 15 seconds; and (d) explain in one sentence each why a firewall is not an antivirus, why a padlock does not mean a safe website, and why a Trojan is not a virus. Two consecutive Sundays meeting all four means this topic goes to weekly maintenance and stops consuming study time.
questionPatterns: Q: Which of the following is a self-replicating malicious program that spreads across a computer network on its own, without attaching itself to a host file and without any action by the user? (a) Virus (b) Trojan horse (c) Worm (d) Adware (e) Rootkit — ANSWER: (c) Worm. A virus needs a host file plus user execution; a Trojan does not replicate at all.

Q: In public-key cryptography, if Ravi wants to send a confidential message to Sneha so that only Sneha can read it, the message must be encrypted using — (a) Ravi's private key (b) Ravi's public key (c) Sneha's private key (d) Sneha's public key (e) a secret key shared publicly on the network — ANSWER: (d) Sneha's public key; she alone holds the matching private key to decrypt it.

Q: A digital signature attached to an electronic document is created using — (a) the receiver's public key (b) the sender's private key (c) the receiver's private key (d) a symmetric session key (e) the Certifying Authority's private key — ANSWER: (b) the sender's private key. It provides authenticity, integrity and non-repudiation.

Q: A customer receives an SMS claiming her bank account will be blocked and asking her to click a link and enter her card details. This form of fraud is called — (a) Phishing (b) Vishing (c) Smishing (d) Pharming (e) Shoulder surfing — ANSWER: (c) Smishing, because the channel is SMS.

Q: An attack in which a large number of compromised computers, controlled remotely as a botnet, simultaneously flood a server so that genuine users cannot access it, is known as — (a) DoS attack (b) DDoS attack (c) Man-in-the-middle attack (d) SQL injection (e) Phishing attack — ANSWER: (b) DDoS; the word 'distributed' signals multiple attacking machines.

Q: The padlock symbol shown beside a website address in a browser indicates that — (a) the website is certified as genuine and safe by the Government (b) the website cannot contain any malware (c) the connection between the browser and the website is encrypted (d) the website does not use cookies (e) the website is free of advertisements — ANSWER: (c). The padlock certifies the encrypted connection, not the honesty of the site.

Q: Which of the following is primarily designed to monitor and control incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined security rules? (a) Antivirus software (b) Firewall (c) Digital certificate (d) Cookie manager (e) Disk defragmenter — ANSWER: (b) Firewall.

Q: A person who breaks into a computer system without the owner's permission but does so to expose weaknesses rather than to cause harm is called a — (a) White hat hacker (b) Black hat hacker (c) Grey hat hacker (d) Script kiddie (e) Phreaker — ANSWER: (c) Grey hat hacker: no permission, but no malicious intent.

comp-security.aiPrompt: Act as an IBPS Clerk Mains paper setter for the Reasoning Ability & Computer Aptitude section. Generate 20 Computer Awareness questions on computer security. EVERY question must have exactly FIVE options labelled (a) to (e) — IBPS papers have five options, never four. comp-security.blockPlan:
Computer Awareness is a support topic, not a main course: cap it at 20-25 minutes a day inside your 4-hour block, ideally in the low-energy slot after lunch or as the last 20 minutes of the night, never in your peak morning hour which belongs to puzzles and DI.
WEEK 1 — Day 1: 60 minutes, one sitting, handwrite the full A4 sheet (Boxes 1-6 plus the back page). This is the only long session this topic ever gets. Day 2: 15 minutes reading the sheet aloud, then 20 questions from a question bank. Day 3: 15 minutes, cover the NAME column and do the reversal drill on Boxes 1 and 2. Day 4-6: 15 minutes each — one box per day plus 15 questions. Day 7: 20-minute full-sheet revision plus the first Sunday timed drill (30 terms, 8 minutes).
WEEK 2-3 — 12 minutes a day: read one box, do 15 mixed questions, add every miss to the error strip. Sunday: timed drill plus a 40-question mixed computer set with a stopwatch, checking that no computer question crosses 20 seconds.
WEEK 4 ONWARDS — maintenance only: two sessions a week of 10 minutes (sheet) plus one Sunday drill. Merge these into your General Awareness revision slot since both are pure recall and the same spaced-repetition rhythm serves both.
LAST 10 DAYS BEFORE 27 DECEMBER — read the error strip only, 5 minutes daily. Do not re-read the full sheet and do not add new material; new security terms picked up in December displace things you already own.
SECTIONAL PRACTICE RULE: in every full Reasoning & Computer Aptitude mock (40 questions, 35 minutes), attempt the computer questions FIRST, finish all of them in under 90 seconds, then start the puzzles. That habit is worth more than any extra fact, because the marks these questions protect are the puzzle marks you now have time to attempt.

comp-database.topicName: Database Basics and the Standard Abbreviation List
comp-database.whatItIs: Two recall blocks that IBPS treats as one. The database half covers DBMS versus RDBMS, the vocabulary of a table (record/tuple/row, field/attribute/column, cardinality, degree), the key family (primary, candidate, alternate, super, composite, foreign), the four SQL command categories (DDL, DML, DCL, TCL) with their commands, normalisation at the level of naming what 1NF/2NF/3NF/BCNF remove, and the data-versus-information distinction. The abbreviation half is the standing full-form list that every Indian banking paper draws from — CPU, ALU, GUI, HTTP, URL, ISP, LAN, RAM, ROM, USB, PDF, ASCII, BIOS, HTML, IP, WWW, MODEM, OCR, OMR, SIM, GPS and around eighty relatives. Both halves are pure lookup. There is no reasoning step: the mark is decided entirely by whether the item is already in memory, and the only skill worth building is retrieval speed under 15 seconds.
comp-database.coreMethod:
1. Build TWO sheets, kept separate because they are revised at different speeds. Sheet A = database concepts, one side of A4. Sheet B = abbreviations, one side of A4 in three narrow columns, roughly 90 entries. Handwrite both.
2. SHEET A, BLOCK 1 — the vocabulary equivalences, written as an equals-chain so you never lose one: Table = Relation = File; Row = Record = Tuple; Column = Field = Attribute; Number of ROWS = CARDINALITY; Number of COLUMNS = DEGREE; the set of permitted values for a column = DOMAIN. One line under it: E. F. Codd proposed the relational model (1970) and the 12 rules.
3. SHEET A, BLOCK 2 — DBMS vs RDBMS, four contrast lines: DBMS stores data as files with little or no relationship between them; RDBMS stores data in TABLES and enforces relationships through keys; RDBMS supports normalisation, integrity constraints and multiple users; every RDBMS is a DBMS but not every DBMS is an RDBMS. Examples: MS Access, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, PostgreSQL, DB2 are RDBMS; a plain file system is not.
4. SHEET A, BLOCK 3 — the key family, one line each, definitions written so that they cannot be confused: SUPER KEY = any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row; CANDIDATE KEY = a minimal super key (no redundant attribute); PRIMARY KEY = the ONE candidate key chosen by the designer, must be UNIQUE and NOT NULL, only one per table; ALTERNATE KEY = the candidate keys not chosen as primary; COMPOSITE KEY = a key made of two or more columns; FOREIGN KEY = a column in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, and it MAY be null and MAY repeat. Write that last clause in capitals — it is the trap.
5. SHEET A, BLOCK 4 — SQL categories as a four-row table you can reproduce blind: DDL (Data Definition Language) = CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME — changes structure, auto-committed; DML (Data Manipulation Language) = INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and SELECT (often listed separately as DQL) — changes data, can be rolled back; DCL (Data Control Language) = GRANT, REVOKE — permissions; TCL (Transaction Control Language) = COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT — transactions. Under the table write the DELETE/TRUNCATE/DROP comparison in three lines because it is asked more often than anything else in SQL.
6. SHEET A, BLOCK 5 — normalisation by name only, since Clerk level never asks you to normalise: purpose = reduce redundancy and remove insert/update/delete anomalies; 1NF = every value atomic, no repeating groups; 2NF = 1NF plus no partial dependency on part of a composite key; 3NF = 2NF plus no transitive dependency; BCNF = a stricter 3NF; 4NF = removes multivalued dependencies. Then: Data = raw unprocessed facts; Information = data that has been processed and given meaning; the chain is Data → Processing → Information → Knowledge.
7. SHEET B — abbreviations grouped by FAMILY, never alphabetically. Alphabetical lists are unrevisable. Use six families: (i) HARDWARE — CPU Central Processing Unit, ALU Arithmetic Logic Unit, CU Control Unit, RAM Random Access Memory, ROM Read Only Memory, PROM Programmable ROM, EPROM Erasable PROM, EEPROM Electrically Erasable PROM, HDD Hard Disk Drive, SSD Solid State Drive, USB Universal Serial Bus, UPS Uninterruptible Power Supply, SMPS Switched Mode Power Supply, NIC Network Interface Card, BIOS Basic Input Output System, POST Power On Self Test, VDU Visual Display Unit. (ii) INPUT/OUTPUT AND SCANNING — OCR Optical Character Recognition, OMR Optical Mark Recognition/Reader, MICR Magnetic Ink Character Recognition, LED, LCD, OLED, CRT, DPI Dots Per Inch. (iii) NETWORK AND INTERNET — LAN Local Area Network, MAN Metropolitan Area Network, WAN Wide Area Network, PAN Personal Area Network, HTTP HyperText Transfer Protocol, HTTPS HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure, HTML HyperText Markup Language, URL Uniform Resource Locator, IP Internet Protocol, TCP Transmission Control Protocol, UDP User Datagram Protocol, FTP File Transfer Protocol, SMTP Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, POP Post Office Protocol, IMAP Internet Message Access Protocol, DNS Domain Name System, DHCP Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol, ISP Internet Service Provider, WWW World Wide Web, VPN Virtual Private Network, VoIP Voice over Internet Protocol, MODEM Modulator-Demodulator, ISDN Integrated Services Digital Network, GSM Global System for Mobile communication, SIM Subscriber Identity Module, GPS Global Positioning System, MAC Media Access Control. (iv) SOFTWARE AND FILES — OS Operating System, GUI Graphical User Interface, CLI Command Line Interface, PDF Portable Document Format, DOC, JPEG Joint Photographic Experts Group, GIF Graphics Interchange Format, PNG Portable Network Graphics, MPEG Moving Picture Experts Group, ASCII American Standard Code for Information Interchange, EBCDIC, BCD Binary Coded Decimal, ANSI, ISO. (v) DATABASE AND LANGUAGES — DBMS, RDBMS, SQL Structured Query Language, DDL, DML, DCL, TCL, DBA Database Administrator, ER Entity-Relationship, COBOL Common Business Oriented Language, FORTRAN Formula Translation, BASIC Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code, CAD Computer Aided Design. (vi) MISCELLANEOUS — ATM Automated Teller Machine, PIN Personal Identification Number, IoT Internet of Things, AI Artificial Intelligence, KB/MB/GB/TB.
8. REVISION RHYTHM, different for the two sheets: Sheet A (concepts) on Day 0, 1, 3, 7, 15, 30 then weekly. Sheet B (abbreviations) needs more frequent, shorter contact — 4 minutes daily for the first three weeks, then every alternate day, then twice weekly. Abbreviations decay faster than concepts.
9. SELF-TEST BY REVERSAL, both directions: (i) cover the expansion column and expand each abbreviation aloud; (ii) harder and more exam-like, read the expansion and name the abbreviation. Do the second direction every third session.
10. ERROR STRIP: any abbreviation you miss twice gets copied onto a separate slip. By exam week the slip should hold 15-20 items, and that slip is your final revision, not the 90-entry sheet.
11. TIMED DRILL every Sunday: 40 abbreviations in 6 minutes (9 seconds each) plus 10 database concept prompts in 3 minutes. Anything slower than 15 seconds goes on the strip.
tricks: ROWS/COLUMNS mapped by shape: CARDINALITY has the sound of 'counting cards' laid in a stack — cards stack in ROWS, so cardinality = number of rows/tuples. DEGREE relates to columns (think of a column of degrees on a thermometer). Get this pair straight once and two exam questions become automatic.

KEY LADDER, narrated in one breath: 'Super key is any unique set → strip the extra columns and it becomes a Candidate key → the designer picks one Candidate as the Primary key → the leftover candidates are Alternate keys.' Recite the ladder rather than four separate definitions; the exam almost always asks which rung a description sits on.

FOREIGN KEY freedom: the primary key is the strict one (unique AND not null); the foreign key is the relaxed one (may be null, may repeat). Remember 'the primary is strict at home, the foreign is free.' Candidates lose marks by assuming a foreign key must also be unique.

SQL FOUR-LETTER CUE: DDL = Definition (structure), DML = Manipulation (data), DCL = Control (permissions — GRANT and REVOKE only), TCL = Transaction (COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT). The second letter of each abbreviation IS the meaning. GRANT/REVOKE is the smallest list and therefore the easiest question in the topic.

DELETE-TRUNCATE-DROP staircase: DELETE removes chosen rows (DML, can be rolled back), TRUNCATE removes ALL rows but keeps the empty table (DDL, auto-commit), DROP removes the table itself, structure included (DDL). Picture emptying a cupboard shelf by shelf, emptying the whole cupboard, then throwing the cupboard out.

NORMAL FORM STAIRCASE: 1NF kills repeating groups (Atomic), 2NF kills Partial dependency, 3NF kills Transitive dependency. Mnemonic: A-P-T, in order, one word per form. Clerk level only ever asks which form removes which dependency.

GROUP ABBREVIATIONS BY FUNCTION, NEVER ALPHABETICALLY. Recalling 'the mail protocols' pulls SMTP, POP and IMAP together in one movement, whereas an A-to-Z list gives you nothing to pull on. This grouping is worth more than any single mnemonic on this sheet.

MAIL DIRECTION: SMTP has an S for Send; POP and IMAP both start with a vowel and both bring mail IN (POP downloads and typically removes from the server, IMAP keeps it synchronised on the server). One line settles a recurring question.

NETWORK SIZE LADDER: PAN (about 10 metres, Bluetooth) → LAN (one building or campus, up to roughly 1-2 km) → MAN (one city, roughly 5-50 km) → WAN (country or worldwide, no limit). Say it as a place: desk → building → city → country.

BACKRONYM HONESTY, so you are not surprised: 'Wireless Fidelity' for Wi-Fi and 'Vital Information Resources Under Siege' for VIRUS are backronyms — the Wi-Fi Alliance states Wi-Fi is a trademark and not an acronym, and VIRUS is not a true abbreviation. Indian exam keys nevertheless print these expansions. Learn both the fact and the expansion, and if that expansion appears among the five options it is the one the key intends.
traps: PRIMARY KEY vs CANDIDATE KEY vs SUPER KEY: a table can have several candidate keys but only ONE primary key. A super key need not be minimal. The question 'a minimal super key is called' answers to candidate key, not primary key.

PRIMARY vs FOREIGN KEY nullability: primary key can never be null and never repeat; a foreign key can be null and can repeat. Options asserting that a foreign key must be unique are planted distractors.
CARDINALITY vs DEGREE: cardinality = rows, degree = columns. Reversing these is the most common single error in this module.

DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP: DELETE is DML and can be rolled back; TRUNCATE is DDL, removes all rows and auto-commits; DROP removes the table structure entirely. All three will sit in the same five options.

SELECT's category: SELECT is a DML command in the traditional four-way split but is classified as DQL (Data Query Language) in the five-way split. If both DML and DQL appear as options for SELECT, DQL is the more specific and intended answer; if DQL is absent, DML is correct.
DCL commands: DCL is ONLY GRANT and REVOKE. COMMIT and ROLLBACK are TCL, not DCL. This swap appears every year.

DBMS vs RDBMS: not every DBMS is relational. MS Access, Oracle and MySQL are RDBMS; a flat file system is a data store but not an RDBMS. Also, 'RDBMS stores data in tables' is the defining property, not 'RDBMS is faster'.
NORMAL FORM MIX-UP: 2NF removes PARTIAL dependency, 3NF removes TRANSITIVE dependency. Reversing these two words is the standard error.
DATA vs INFORMATION: data is raw and unprocessed; information is processed data with meaning. An option calling information 'raw facts' is wrong even though it reads plausibly.
HTTP vs HTML: HTTP is the transfer PROTOCOL, HTML is the markup LANGUAGE for writing the page. Both appear together in the same options.

URL vs IP ADDRESS vs DOMAIN NAME: a URL is the full address of a resource; a domain name is the human-readable site name; an IP address is the numeric address; DNS is the system that translates between them.

OCR vs OMR vs MICR vs BARCODE READER: OCR reads printed or typed CHARACTERS; OMR detects MARKS such as filled bubbles on an answer sheet; MICR reads characters printed in magnetic ink on cheques; a barcode reader reads bars. IBPS loves putting all four in one question, usually with an OMR answer-sheet scenario.

RAM vs ROM: RAM is volatile, read-write, temporary working memory; ROM is non-volatile, essentially read-only, holds firmware such as the BIOS. Also note the PROM/EPROM/EEPROM ladder — EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light, EEPROM electrically.

LAN vs MAN vs WAN ranges: a question giving a distance or a scope ('across a city', 'within a single building', 'across countries') is testing the ladder, and MAN is the option candidates forget exists.
TCP vs UDP: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable with acknowledgements; UDP is connectionless, faster and unreliable. Both are transport-layer protocols and both will be offered.

ASCII vs EBCDIC vs UNICODE: ASCII is a 7-bit American standard code (extended ASCII is 8-bit); Unicode is the multilingual standard. Expanding ASCII wrongly as 'American Standard Code for Information Exchange' instead of 'Interchange' costs the mark when both variants are printed as options.
comp-database.timeTarget: 8-15 seconds. An abbreviation question is either instant or unknown — there is nothing to work out, so give it one read and one glance at the five options. A database concept question deserves at most 15 seconds because the distinction being tested (rows vs columns, DDL vs DML, primary vs foreign) is binary once recalled. Do not spend 30 seconds reasoning about which SQL category a command belongs to; if the four-row table did not surface, leave it, since 0.25 negative makes a five-way guess unprofitable.
comp-database.masteryCheck: You own this module when, cold and timed, you can (a) write the four-row SQL table — all four categories with at least three commands each — from a blank page in under 90 seconds with no misplacement; (b) state the key ladder (super → candidate → primary → alternate) plus the two foreign-key freedoms in under 30 seconds; (c) expand 40 abbreviations in 6 minutes with 38 or more correct, and separately go the harder direction, naming the abbreviation from its expansion, at 35 or more out of 40; and (d) answer, without hesitation, cardinality-vs-degree, 2NF-vs-3NF, DELETE-vs-TRUNCATE and OCR-vs-OMR. Hit all four on two consecutive Sundays and drop to weekly maintenance.
questionPatterns: Q: In a relational database, the number of ROWS (tuples) in a table is known as its — (a) Degree (b) Domain (c) Cardinality (d) Attribute (e) Schema — ANSWER: (c) Cardinality. The number of columns is the degree.

Q: Which of the following SQL commands belongs to the Data Definition Language (DDL) category? (a) UPDATE (b) GRANT (c) TRUNCATE (d) COMMIT (e) INSERT — ANSWER: (c) TRUNCATE. UPDATE and INSERT are DML, GRANT is DCL, COMMIT is TCL.
Q: GRANT and REVOKE are commands belonging to which category of SQL? (a) DDL (b) DML (c) DCL (d) TCL (e) DQL — ANSWER: (c) DCL, Data Control Language, which deals only with permissions.

Q: A column in one table that refers to the primary key of another table is called a — (a) Candidate key (b) Composite key (c) Super key (d) Foreign key (e) Alternate key — ANSWER: (d) Foreign key. Unlike a primary key, it may contain null and duplicate values.

Q: Which normal form eliminates transitive dependency? (a) First Normal Form (b) Second Normal Form (c) Third Normal Form (d) Boyce-Codd Normal Form (e) Fourth Normal Form — ANSWER: (c) Third Normal Form. 2NF removes partial dependency; 1NF removes repeating groups.

Q: ASCII stands for — (a) American Standard Code for Information Interchange (b) American Standard Code for Information Exchange (c) Advanced Standard Code for Internet Interchange (d) American System Code for Information Interchange (e) Automatic Standard Code for Information Interchange — ANSWER: (a). The word is Interchange, and the first word is American, not Advanced.

Q: The device used to read pencil marks made in the bubbles of a competitive examination answer sheet is — (a) OCR (b) MICR (c) OMR (d) Barcode reader (e) Light pen — ANSWER: (c) OMR, Optical Mark Recognition. OCR reads printed characters; MICR reads magnetic-ink characters on cheques.

Q: Which of the following is a volatile memory whose contents are lost when the computer is switched off? (a) ROM (b) PROM (c) EPROM (d) RAM (e) Hard disk — ANSWER: (d) RAM. ROM and its variants are non-volatile.
Q: A network that spans a single city and typically covers a range of about 5 to 50 kilometres is called a — (a) LAN (b) PAN (c) MAN (d) WAN (e) VPN — ANSWER: (c) MAN, Metropolitan Area Network.

Q: Raw, unprocessed facts and figures that by themselves carry no meaning are referred to as — (a) Information (b) Knowledge (c) Data (d) Report (e) Record — ANSWER: (c) Data. Information is data that has been processed and given meaning.
